reading.synopsis: Bob Clarke is called up for another tour fighting the Martians over rexeroid, a mineral essential to his household's automated control systems, and offers his wife Joan a matter-of-fact economic justification: without rexeroid, kryon, or lonolite, ordinary technological comforts (car steering, climate-controlled walls, computer memory) would collapse. Bob never returns from Mars. Their son Tommy takes his place, first fighting the Callisto gleco-war for door-lock material, then dying in the Europa trektone-war over vidscreen components. Sector Organizer Bryan Erickson keeps appearing at Joan's door with each new escalation, eventually informing her that women are now being drafted too, as the wars for iderium, ambroline, and finally nymphite consume an ever-larger share of the population defending an ever-more-elaborate structure of consumer conveniences. The story ends generations later, after humanity has apparently died out entirely: two alien explorers from Orion land on an empty, overgrown Earth, discover an advanced, fully automated house with no occupants, and wait patiently for the 'Terrans' to return, unaware there is no one left to come back.

structure.form: short story in escalating repeated cycles, each one substituting a new family member, a new planet, and a new essential mineral, followed by a coda from an entirely alien perspective
movements: Bob is drafted to fight for rexeroid on Mars and never returns, each household convenience justified as a reason the war must continue.
Tommy takes his father's place, escalating through further wars (gleco, trektone) until he too is killed, and the draft is extended to women as losses mount.
Told from the perspective of two Orionian explorers arriving long after humanity's presumed extinction, the story closes on their patient, uncomprehending wait for 'Terrans' who will never return.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Joan through the escalating cycle of loss, then an abrupt final shift to the alien explorers' perspective, which knows nothing of the preceding history and can only observe its empty result.
structure.central_device: A structurally repeating draft cycle in which each new war is justified by an increasingly trivial household convenience, so that the human cost of maintaining a comfortable technological civilization is made explicit and cumulative rather than abstract, ending in a species wiped out entirely by its own inability to question the premise.

characters.name: Joan Clarke
characters.role: wife and mother, the story's emotional center
characters.note: Her repeated, quietly probing questions ('Why do we have to fight the Martians?', 'Who will be left?') are the story's only voice of doubt, and change nothing about the outcome — she loses husband, then son, and is finally drafted herself.

characters.name: Bob Clarke
characters.note: Offers the story's first and clearest articulation of its central logic: technological comfort justifies endless resource war, however trivial the resource, because giving up the comfort feels unthinkable.

characters.name: Tommy Clarke
characters.note: Inherits his father's uniform, his father's war, and eventually his father's fate, presented by the story as an unremarkable, almost proud continuation of duty rather than as tragedy repeating itself.

characters.name: Bryan Erickson
characters.note: A recurring, sympathetic-seeming bureaucratic messenger, delivering each fresh escalation with genuine discomfort but never once questioning the system he administers.

characters.name: N'tgari-3 and Luci'n-6
characters.note: Arrive with no knowledge of Earth's history, mistake its automated infrastructure for evidence of 'an advanced culture,' and wait indefinitely for inhabitants who no longer exist — the story's final, coldly ironic punctuation mark.

settings.name: The Clarke household
settings.note: A marvel of automation (bed-makers, meal selectors, automatic sorters) whose conveniences are each, one by one, revealed as the specific justification for a specific war and a specific death.

settings.name: Empty, overgrown Earth
settings.note: The story's final setting inverts the entire preceding narrative — the technological civilization so fiercely defended survives intact as physical infrastructure while the species that built and fought for it has vanished.

motifs: An escalating sequence of wars, each justified by an increasingly minor technological convenience, mapped onto a widening resource-extraction empire across the solar system
A household's automated comforts (steering, climate control, computing, door locks, news, aptitude testing, entertainment) each individually indispensable and collectively fatal
A woman's repeated, unanswerable questions serving as the story's only form of resistance, changing nothing
A closing perspective shift to alien outsiders who cannot perceive the tragedy they are standing in the middle of
Colonial extraction logic explicitly mapped onto encounters with 'natives' on multiple planets, treated with the same dismissive brevity throughout
reading.significance: The story's real subject is the normalization of endless war through the accumulation of small, individually reasonable justifications — no single convenience (better steering, temperature control, computer memory, door locks, unbiased news, entertainment, aptitude testing) seems worth dying for, yet the sum of all of them consumes an entire species. Joan's escalating losses are narrated with almost no editorializing, letting the sheer repetition of Erickson's visits do the story's argumentative work. The final alien perspective, arriving in genuine ignorance and simply waiting for a species that will never return, denies the reader any survivor's vantage point from which to properly mourn what has happened — the only witnesses left don't know there is anything to witness.
reading.closing_note: N'tgari-3's earnest, hopeful insistence — 'I have a feeling they won't [return]... I'll keep watching for them' — closes the story on dramatic irony rather than grief, the full weight of the preceding tragedy legible only to the reader.

distinctive_terms.label: House
distinctive_terms.note: The household and its automated comforts are the story's recurring, literal stakes for every successive war.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: an escalating, multi-planet resource-extraction war economy that consumes an entire species one household convenience at a time, extending conscription from men to sons to, finally, women
the story's closing perspective shift to alien explorers discovering Earth's advanced but entirely depopulated infrastructure, waiting in ignorance for inhabitants who no longer exist
